summary: This is a genuine whitespace opportunity with validated demand behavior but weak monetization signals. Users demonstrably care about tracking Stack Exchange reputation over time — they sustain painful manual spreadsheet logging (SIG-002) and build entire ecosystems of DIY scripts, userscripts, and SEDE queries to approximate the JTBD. Yet no purpose-built product exists: every alternative is either raw infrastructure (SEDE, API), a current-snapshot partial solution (iOS widget), a fragile hack (userscripts), or the manual status quo. Adjacent categories (GitHub stats cards, Dev.to analytics) prove this exact audience adopts personal-metric visualization tools. The bull case rests on being first to productize an obviously desired workflow with near-zero data costs — but it is tempered by the lowest possible willingness-to-pay and urgency scores and a single-item evidence base.
strongest_points: Workaround behavior validates real demand: SIG-002 confirms users manually copy-paste reputation data into spreadsheets on a daily/weekly cadence — a high-friction, error-prone ritual people only sustain when they genuinely value the outcome. The case file further documents users building scripts around the Stack Exchange API and explicitly frames this as 'evidence of unmet need, not a competing solution.'

Total product whitespace (competition score 2): every documented competitor fails the JTBD in a distinct way — SEDE requires SQL knowledge with no visualization, scheduling, or one-click multi-site aggregation; the API is raw developer infrastructure; the iOS Super User Widget shows current snapshots only with no history or export; StackApps userscripts are browser-bound, fragile, and lack export/persistence; GitHub-hosted scripts are fragmented hobbyist one-offs; and Google Sheets/Excel is the painful status quo (SIG-002). No commercial product offers automated, multi-site, historical reputation tracking with visualization — a first mover faces zero direct product competition.

Adjacent-category validation de-risks the demand thesis: GitHub Readme Stats, GitHub Skyline, and Shields.io SE badges demonstrate that this exact audience (developers who write and care about quantified reputation) actively adopts personal-metric visualization — and some already surface static Stack Overflow reputation in their profiles, proving desire to display SE reputation off-platform. Dev.to/Hashnode built-in analytics confirm developer-writers engage with performance dashboards. The missing piece across all of these is precisely the historical trend tracking this product delivers.

Near-zero data COGS and a pre-identified, reachable buyer: the official Stack Exchange API provides free reputation-history endpoints, so the core data input costs nothing. Target users are concentrated and self-identifying — they congregate on StackApps, Meta Stack Exchange, and the very GitHub repos/userscripts catalogued in the case file — creating a low-CAC distribution channel of users who have already demonstrated the painful behavior (SIG-002).

Compounding retention and switching-cost mechanics: historical data accumulates value the longer a user tracks, making their dataset increasingly irreplaceable and raising switching costs post-adoption. Automating a recurring manual chore (SIG-002) into scheduled tracking, cross-site aggregation, alerts, and export creates genuine recurring value — the raw material for subscription revenue and the global applicability score of 3 (the highest in the validation set) indicates the audience is not geographically constrained.
weaknesses: Willingness to pay scored 1 — the weakest possible signal — and every existing alternative is free. The target user (a technical power user) is precisely the demographic most capable of DIY-ing a solution with SEDE or the API, which severely caps monetization.

Urgency and economic impact both scored 1: reputation tracking is a vanity/curiosity metric for most users with no direct tie to income or business outcomes, implying high price sensitivity and churn risk even if adoption occurs.

The evidence base is a single item (SIG-002). No market size data exists in the case file, so TAM cannot be honestly claimed, and pain intensity (2) and frequency (2) indicate even believers feel this pain mildly and infrequently.

Total platform dependency: the product lives entirely on Stack Exchange's API, rate limits, and continued platform health. An API change, pricing shift, or decline in SE engagement is an existential threat with no mitigation.

The most engaged potential users have already partially solved the problem for themselves via scripts and SEDE queries, meaning the easiest-to-reach segment may be the hardest to convert to paying customers.
